title: Carbonyl compounds
objectives: Recall that aldehydes are made by oxidising primary alcohols (distilling) and ketones by oxidising secondary alcohols
Describe the reduction of aldehydes and ketones with NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄
Describe the reaction of aldehydes and ketones with HCN (KCN catalyst) and the mechanism of nucleophilic addition
Use 2,4-DNPH reagent to detect a carbonyl group
Use Tollens’ reagent and Fehling’s reagent to distinguish aldehydes from ketones
Use alkaline I₂(aq) to detect the CH₃CO– group, and deduce structures from test results
prior: Oxidation of alcohols and the tri-iodomethane test (Chapter 16)
why: The C=O group is the most important functional group in organic synthesis: it can be reduced, extended by one carbon with HCN, and identified with simple tests. Paper 2 almost always asks for the nucleophilic addition mechanism, and Paper 1 tests the identification reagents every session.
intro: Aldehydes (RCHO) have the C=O at the end of a chain, with an H on the carbonyl carbon; ketones (RCOR′) have it within the chain. The C=O bond is polar (Cδ+=Oδ−) and its carbon is trigonal planar, so nucleophiles can attack it from either side.

blocks.cap: From alcohols to carbonyls and back
head: change
reagent and conditions
example
rows: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, warm; distil off the aldehyde as it forms
NaBH₄ (aqueous or in methanol) or LiAlH₄ (dry ether)

blocks.h: In equations, [H] stands for a hydrogen atom from the reducing agent. Both hydrides deliver H⁻, a nucleophile, to the δ+ carbon. NaBH₄ is milder and safer; only LiAlH₄ also reduces carboxylic acids.

Aldehydes and ketones react with HCN, with a little KCN as catalyst, at room temperature. The product is a hydroxynitrile, with one more carbon atom: CH₃CHO + HCN → CH₃CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile).

items: Step 1: the lone pair on the C of CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; the π electrons of C=O move onto O, forming an alkoxide intermediate R₂C(O⁻)CN.
Step 2: the O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN, giving R₂C(OH)CN and regenerating CN⁻ (so CN⁻ is a catalyst).
KCN is used because HCN is a weak acid and gives too little CN⁻ on its own.

blocks.name: nucadd
blocks.title: Nucleophilic addition, step by step
blocks.h: Step through the mechanism for different carbonyl compounds and see whether the product is chiral.

If the two groups on the C=O are different (any aldehyde except methanal; an unsymmetrical ketone), the product has a chiral carbon. Because the carbonyl group is planar, CN⁻ attacks from above and below equally, giving a racemic mixture (no optical activity). Propanone gives an achiral product.
The –CN group can then be hydrolysed (heat with dilute acid) to –COOH, giving a 2-hydroxycarboxylic acid: a useful way to lengthen a carbon chain.

blocks.wrong: In HCN addition, H⁺ attacks the oxygen first.
blocks.right: The nucleophile CN⁻ attacks the carbon first; the proton is added to O⁻ in the second step.

blocks.h: Aldehydes have an H on the carbonyl carbon, so mild oxidising agents can turn them into carboxylic acids. Ketones have no such H and resist mild oxidation. Methanoic acid, HCOOH, also contains H–C=O and gives positive Tollens’ and Fehling’s tests.

blocks.name: carbtest
blocks.title: Carbonyl test lab
blocks.h: Choose a compound and a reagent; the table below shows its full set of results.

blocks.q: C₅H₁₀O gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, no change with Tollens’ reagent and a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq). Suggest two possible structures.
steps: methyl ketones C₅H₁₀O: CH₃CO–C₃H₇ with propyl or methylethyl
blocks.err: Including pentan-3-one, which has no CH₃CO– group.

sections.title: The tri-iodomethane test and deducing structures

blocks.h: Alkaline I₂(aq) gives yellow CHI₃ with any compound containing CH₃CO– (ethanal and methyl ketones), or a group it can oxidise to this, CH₃CH(OH)–. The rest of the molecule ends up as a carboxylate ion: CH₃COR → CHI₃ + RCOO⁻.

items: Propanone → CHI₃ + CH₃COO⁻; butanone → CHI₃ + CH₃CH₂COO⁻.
Acidifying afterwards turns RCOO⁻ into RCOOH.
Ethanal is the only aldehyde that is positive.
Tollens’ / Fehling’s positive? → aldehyde; negative → ketone.
Yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂? → CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)–.
Fizz with Na? → O–H present (alcohol or acid).
Use combustion data or Mr to fix the number of carbons.

summary: Aldehyde RCHO (C=O at chain end); ketone RCOR′ (C=O within chain). C=O is polar and planar.
Primary alcohol → aldehyde (distil); secondary → ketone. NaBH₄/LiAlH₄ reduce them back.
HCN + KCN catalyst → hydroxynitrile (+1 C) by nucleophilic addition: CN⁻ attacks C, then O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN.
Planar C=O → attack from either side → racemic mixture when the product is chiral.
Tollens’ (silver mirror) and Fehling’s (red-brown Cu₂O) are positive only for aldehydes.
Alkaline I₂: yellow CHI₃ with CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)–; the rest becomes RCOO⁻.
Ketones are not oxidised by dichromate, Tollens’ or Fehling’s.

flash.q: Which give positive Tollens’: aldehydes or ketones?
Why are ketones not oxidised by Tollens’?
flash.a: No H on the carbonyl carbon

flash.q: Product of NaBH₄ with a ketone?
Product of NaBH₄ with an aldehyde?
Why is KCN added to HCN?
flash.a: Provides CN⁻ nucleophile (HCN is a weak acid); CN⁻ is regenerated (catalyst)

flash.q: Why is the HCN product of ethanal racemic?
flash.a: Planar C=O attacked equally from both sides

flash.q: Products of propanone with alkaline I₂?
Only aldehyde positive with alkaline I₂?

practice.q: Describe the mechanism for the reaction of propanone with HCN, catalysed by KCN.
practice.a: C=O polar; CN⁻ lone pair (on C) attacks δ+ C; π bond electrons move to O giving (CH₃)₂C(O⁻)CN; O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN giving (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN and CN⁻.

practice.q: Describe two chemical tests to distinguish propanal from propanone.
practice.a: Tollens’ reagent: propanal gives a silver mirror, propanone no change. Alkaline I₂: propanone gives a yellow precipitate, propanal none. (Fehling’s or dichromate also work.)

practice.q: Write an equation for the reduction of butanone and name the product.
Explain why the product of butanal and HCN is not optically active although it has a chiral centre.
practice.a: The C=O is planar, so CN⁻ attacks from both sides with equal probability, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers (racemic mixture).

practice.q: Give the products when butanone is warmed with alkaline I₂(aq).
C₄H₈O gives an orange 2,4-DNPH precipitate and a silver mirror. Give two possible structures.

assessment.q: Which reagent gives an orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones?
Ketones give a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent.
assessment.why: No H on the C=O carbon.

assessment.q: Which atom of CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon?
Which gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂?

assessment.why: OH and CN on the old C=O carbon.

assessment.q: Which reduces a ketone but would also reduce a carboxylic acid?
assessment.why: LiAlH₄ is the stronger reducing agent.

assessment_s.q:
Compound A, C₃H₆O, gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent.
(a) Identify A. [1]
(b) A reacts with HCN/KCN. Name the product and the mechanism. [2]
(c) Explain why the product of (b) is not optically active. [2]
(d) Name the isomer of A that gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq), and the organic ion formed. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO
(b) 2-hydroxybutanenitrile; nucleophilic addition
(c) the C=O is planar so CN⁻ attacks equally from either side, giving a racemic (50:50) mixture whose rotations cancel
(d) propanone; ethanoate, CH₃COO⁻

assessment_s.q:
Butanone is reduced and also reacted with HCN.
(a) Give the reducing agent and write the equation using [H]. [2]
(b) Draw the product with HCN and mark the chiral centre. [2]
(c) Give the product formed when the HCN product is heated with dilute HCl. [1]
assessment_s.a:
(a) NaBH₄; CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
(b) CH₃C(OH)(CN)CH₂CH₃; the central C bonded to OH, CN, CH₃ and C₂H₅ is chiral
(c) CH₃C(OH)(COOH)CH₂CH₃, 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanoic acid

pp.skill: Product of reducing an aldehyde
pp.mis: Thinking reduction removes the oxygen completely
pp.stem: What is formed when butanal is warmed with aqueous NaBH₄?
pp.exp: NaBH₄ supplies H⁻ (written [H]): CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH. Aldehydes give primary alcohols; ketones give secondary alcohols.

pp.skill: What NaBH₄ cannot reduce
pp.mis: Thinking NaBH₄ reduces every C=O
pp.stem: The simplest ratio of atoms in X is C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1. Lithium tetrahydridoaluminate reduces X, but sodium tetrahydridoborate does not. Identify X.
pp.exp: NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones but not carboxylic acids, so X is an acid. Ethanoic acid, C₂H₄O₂, has empirical formula CH₂O; propanoic acid is C₃H₆O₂. Methanal would be reduced by NaBH₄.

pp.skill: Using an Mr change on reduction to find a ketone
pp.mis: Forgetting that reduction adds exactly 2 H
pp.stem: X is a non-cyclic ketone with one C=O and no other functional group. On reduction with NaBH₄ the Mr increases by exactly 2.000%. X gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq). Considering structural isomers only, how many ketones could X be?
pp.exp: Reduction adds 2 H (Mr + 2.0), so 2.0 = 2.000% of Mr → Mr = 100: C₆H₁₂O. Methyl ketones CH₃CO–C₄H₉ with the four butyl groups: hexan-2-one, 3-methylpentan-2-one, 4-methylpentan-2-one, 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one = 4.

pp.skill: Recognising oxidation of an organic compound
pp.mis: Calling reduction by NaBH₄ an oxidation
pp.stem: In which reaction is the organic compound oxidised?
pp.exp: Fehling’s reagent oxidises the aldehyde to propanoate (Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu₂O). NaBH₄ reduces; H₂SO₄ dehydrates; NaOH hydrolyses.

pp.skill: Which compound undergoes nucleophilic addition
pp.mis: Choosing an alkene
pp.stem: Which compound can undergo nucleophilic addition?
pp.exp: The C=O bond is polar (Cδ+=Oδ−), so nucleophiles attack the carbon and add across it. Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition; chloroethane undergoes substitution.

pp.skill: The attacking species in HCN addition
pp.mis: Thinking H⁺ attacks first
pp.stem: Butanal reacts with HCN in the presence of a little KCN. Which species first attacks the carbonyl carbon, and what is it?
pp.exp: The lone pair on the C of CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O: nucleophilic addition.

pp.skill: Naming the product of HCN addition
pp.mis: Forgetting that CN adds a carbon atom
pp.stem: Propanal reacts with HCN in the presence of CN⁻ ions. Which row is correct?
pp.exp: CH₃CH₂CHO + HCN → CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CN. Counting the nitrile carbon there are 4 C: 2-hydroxybutanenitrile. The mechanism is nucleophilic addition.

pp.skill: The intermediate in HCN addition
pp.mis: Drawing a carbocation intermediate
pp.stem: Ethanal reacts with HCN, catalysed by CN⁻. Which is the intermediate?
pp.exp: CN⁻ attacks the δ+ C and the π bond pair moves onto O, giving an alkoxide anion CH₃CH(O⁻)CN. This then takes H⁺ from HCN to give the product CH₃CH(OH)CN.

pp.skill: Why CN⁻ is a catalyst
pp.mis: Thinking K⁺ takes part
pp.stem: Propanone reacts with KCN dissolved in HCN. Which statement about the mechanism is correct?
opts: K⁺ is attacked by the O⁻ of the intermediate.
The intermediate removes H⁺ from HCN, regenerating CN⁻.
The first step is protonation of the C=O oxygen by HCN.
The reaction is a nucleophilic substitution.
pp.exp: Step 1: CN⁻ adds to C. Step 2: the O⁻ of the intermediate takes H⁺ from HCN, forming the product and a new CN⁻. Because CN⁻ is regenerated it acts as a catalyst.

pp.skill: Order of events in the HCN mechanism
pp.mis: Putting the proton transfer first
pp.stem: Pentan-3-one reacts with HCN mixed with a little KCN. Which description of the mechanism is correct?
opts: The C=O π bond takes H⁺ from HCN, then CN⁻ attacks.
A lone pair on the C atom of CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon; then the O⁻ formed takes H⁺ from HCN.
A lone pair on the N atom of CN⁻ attacks the δ− oxygen; then H⁺ adds to carbon.
The O lone pair takes H⁺ from HCN, then CN⁻ attacks the δ− carbon.
pp.exp: The nucleophile is the C end of CN⁻, attacking the δ+ carbonyl carbon. The π electrons move to O, forming O⁻, which is then protonated by HCN.

pp.skill: Spotting nucleophilic mechanisms
pp.mis: Calling HBr addition nucleophilic
pp.stem:
Two reactions:
1 propanone with HCN (KCN catalyst)
2 propene with HBr
Which has a nucleophilic mechanism?
pp.exp: 1 is nucleophilic addition (CN⁻ attacks C=O). 2 is electrophilic addition (the C=C attacks δ+ H of HBr).

pp.skill: Carbon count after adding HCN
pp.mis: Forgetting the extra carbon from CN
pp.stem: Q reacts with HCN, with a catalyst, to form R. Each molecule of R contains five carbon atoms. What is Q?
pp.exp: HCN adds one carbon, so Q must be a carbonyl compound with four carbons: butanone. Alcohols and halogenoalkanes do not undergo this addition.

pp.skill: Hydrolysing the HCN addition product
pp.mis: Hydrolysing the OH instead of the CN
pp.stem: The product of ethanal and HCN is heated under reflux with dilute HCl. What is the final organic product?
pp.exp: CH₃CH(OH)CN; acid hydrolysis turns –CN into –COOH, giving 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid).

pp.skill: Oxidation by distillation followed by HCN addition
pp.mis: Assuming the acid forms when distilling
pp.stem: Ethanol is warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and the product is distilled off immediately. The distillate is treated with HCN and a little KCN. What is the organic product?
pp.exp: Distilling removes ethanal before it is oxidised further. Ethanal + HCN → CH₃CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile).

pp.skill: Which reaction gives a chiral product
pp.mis: Missing that butan-2-ol is chiral
pp.stem: Which pair of reagents gives a product containing a chiral carbon atom?
pp.exp: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, has C2 bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅. (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN, ethanol and 2-bromopropane each have no carbon with four different groups.

pp.skill: A carbonyl giving chiral products with both HCN and NaBH₄
pp.mis: Choosing an aldehyde, whose NaBH₄ product is not chiral
pp.stem: Q reacts separately with HCN and with NaBH₄. Both products contain a chiral centre. What is Q?
pp.exp: Pentan-2-one: NaBH₄ → pentan-2-ol (C2 has H, OH, CH₃, C₃H₇); HCN → C(OH)(CN)(CH₃)(C₃H₇). Butanal gives butan-1-ol (not chiral); pentan-3-one has two ethyl groups on C3.

pp.skill: Applying nucleophilic addition to a new nucleophile
pp.mis: Adding the nucleophile to the oxygen
pp.stem: CH₃Li contains the nucleophile CH₃⁻. It reacts with butanone by nucleophilic addition; the anion formed is then protonated. What is the final product?
pp.exp: CH₃⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon and O⁻ is protonated: CH₃CH₂C(OH)(CH₃)₂, a tertiary alcohol, 2-methylbutan-2-ol.

pp.skill: A test positive for aldehydes but not ketones
pp.mis: Choosing 2,4-DNPH, which detects both
pp.stem: Which reagent gives a positive result with propanal but not with propanone?
pp.exp: Tollens’ reagent (silver mirror) is reduced only by aldehydes. 2,4-DNPH and NaBH₄ react with both; alkaline I₂ is positive with propanone only.

pp.skill: Choosing a reagent to distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone
pp.mis: Choosing a reagent that both react with
pp.stem: Which reagent distinguishes butanal from butanone?
pp.exp: Butanal reduces blue Fehling’s to a red-brown Cu₂O precipitate; butanone does not. Both give an orange 2,4-DNPH precipitate and both are reduced by NaBH₄; neither decolourises bromine water.

pp.skill: Test results for a dicarbonyl compound
pp.mis: Thinking two C=O groups cancel each other
pp.stem: Ethanedial, OHC–CHO, is tested with 2,4-DNPH reagent and with Fehling’s reagent. What are the results?
pp.exp: Each end is a –CHO group: a carbonyl (orange 2,4-DNPH precipitate) that is also an aldehyde (red-brown Cu₂O with Fehling’s).

pp.skill: Deducing a structure from three tests
pp.mis: Forgetting dichromate also oxidises alcohols
pp.stem: Compound T: gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH; no reaction with Fehling’s solution; no reaction with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. What is T?
pp.exp: A carbonyl that is not an aldehyde (no Fehling’s) and has no oxidisable OH (no dichromate): a simple ketone, pentan-3-one. CH₃COCH₂CH₂OH would turn dichromate green.

pp.skill: Deducing a hydroxyketone from tests
pp.mis: Choosing the dialdehyde
pp.stem: Compound Y turns acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ from orange to green, has no effect on Fehling’s reagent and gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH. What is Y?
pp.exp: 2,4-DNPH → C=O; no Fehling’s → not an aldehyde (so a ketone); dichromate green → an oxidisable group, here the primary OH. The diketone is not oxidised; the dialdehyde would reduce Fehling’s; the diol has no C=O.

pp.skill: Methanoic acid behaves like an aldehyde
pp.mis: Treating all acids the same
pp.stem: Methanoic acid, HCOOH, is oxidised by the same reagents that oxidise aldehydes. Which compound gives the same observation as HCOOH with Tollens’ reagent?
pp.exp: HCOOH contains an H–C=O group and gives a silver mirror, as does the aldehyde propanal. Ethanoic acid, propanone and methyl ethanoate give no change.

pp.skill: Combining E/Z isomerism with the Fehling test
pp.mis: Choosing a ketone
pp.stem: P has E and Z forms, and when warmed with blue Fehling’s solution a brick-red solid appears. Which is P?
pp.exp: But-2-enal has different groups on each C=C carbon (H/CH₃ and H/CHO), so it shows cis/trans isomerism, and it is an aldehyde. CH₂=… and (CH₃)₂C=… cannot show cis/trans; the ketone does not reduce Fehling’s.

pp.skill: Tracking a group through oxidation
pp.mis: Forgetting the aldehyde is oxidised under reflux
pp.stem: 3-hydroxypropanal, HOCH₂CH₂CHO, is refluxed with plenty of Cr₂O₇²⁻/H⁺ until oxidation is complete, giving Y. Samples of the starting material and of Y are warmed with Fehling’s solution. Which turn(s) brick-red?
pp.exp: Under reflux both the primary OH and the CHO are oxidised to COOH: Y = HOOCCH₂COOH, which has no aldehyde group. X still has its CHO group.

pp.skill: Observations of a ketone with three reagents
pp.mis: Expecting a ketone to be oxidised
pp.stem: An excess of propanone is (1) heated with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, (2) warmed with alkaline I₂(aq), (3) boiled with Fehling’s solution. What is seen in each?
pp.exp: Ketones are not oxidised by dichromate (stays orange) or by Fehling’s (stays blue). Propanone has CH₃CO–, so it gives yellow CHI₃.

pp.skill: The second product of the tri-iodomethane reaction, after acidifying
pp.mis: Giving the ion after acid has been added
pp.stem: Pentan-2-one is warmed with alkaline I₂(aq), then excess dilute H₂SO₄ is added. The organic products are CHI₃ and M. What is M?
pp.exp: CH₃CO–C₃H₇ loses the CH₃ as CHI₃; the rest becomes C₃H₇COO⁻ (butanoate). Excess acid then protonates it to butanoic acid.

pp.skill: Combining reduction and iodoform information
pp.mis: Forgetting that ethanal gives the test
pp.stem: Carbonyl compound X is reduced by NaBH₄ to a primary alcohol, and X gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq). What is X?
pp.exp: A primary alcohol comes from an aldehyde. The only aldehyde with CH₃CO– is ethanal, CH₃CHO.

pp.skill: Using three negative/positive results
pp.mis: Choosing an alcohol, which reacts with Na
pp.stem: X does not react with Tollens’ reagent, gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq) and does not react with sodium. What could X be?
pp.exp: Pentan-2-one: not an aldehyde, has CH₃CO–, and no O–H. Propanal reduces Tollens’; butan-2-ol reacts with Na; pentan-3-one has no CH₃CO–.

pp.skill: Pairs distinguishable by alkaline I₂
pp.mis: Assuming all ketones are positive
pp.stem: Which pair can be distinguished by adding alkaline I₂(aq)?
pp.exp: Butanone (CH₃CO–) gives yellow CHI₃; propanal does not. In the other pairs both compounds are positive.

pp.skill: A compound positive with both Tollens’ and alkaline I₂
pp.mis: Choosing a compound with only one of the groups
pp.stem: Q gives a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent and a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq). What is Q?
pp.exp: CH₃COCHO has both a CH₃CO– group (iodoform) and a –CHO group (Tollens’). The dialdehyde and propanal have no CH₃CO–; butanone has no CHO.

pp.skill: Combining combustion data with tests
pp.mis: Using 22.4 dm³ instead of 24.0 dm³ at room conditions
pp.stem: Complete combustion of 0.10 mol of X gives 9.6 dm³ of CO₂ at room conditions. X gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH but no yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq). What could X be?
pp.exp: 9.6 ÷ 24.0 = 0.40 mol CO₂, so 4 C atoms per molecule. A carbonyl compound (2,4-DNPH) without CH₃CO– (no iodoform): butanal. Butanone gives the iodoform test; butan-1-ol has no C=O.

pp.skill: Counting positives for two tests in a set of isomers
pp.mis: Thinking an alcohol gives a 2,4-DNPH precipitate
pp.stem:
Four isomers of C₄H₈O:
• CH₃COCH₂CH₃
• CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO
• CH₃CH(OH)CH=CH₂
• (CH₃)₂CHCHO
How many give a precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, and how many give a precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq)?
pp.exp: The three carbonyl compounds react with 2,4-DNPH; the unsaturated alcohol does not. Butanone (CH₃CO–) and but-3-en-2-ol (CH₃CH(OH)–) give CHI₃.

pp.skill: Counting carbonyl isomers and their Tollens’ results
pp.mis: Forgetting the stereoisomers of a chiral aldehyde
pp.stem: Structural and stereoisomerism should be considered. Consider all carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones) with formula C₄H₈O. Which statement is correct?
opts: There are three; two give a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent.
There are three; all give a silver mirror.
There are four; two give a silver mirror.
There are three; two give a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq).
pp.exp: Butanal, 2-methylpropanal and butanone: none is chiral, so there are three. The two aldehydes give a silver mirror; only butanone gives CHI₃.

pp.skill: Counting iodoform-positive carbonyls among isomers
pp.mis: Counting every ketone as positive
pp.stem: Consider the seven structurally different aldehydes and ketones with formula C₅H₁₀O. How many give a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq)?
pp.exp: Aldehydes: pentanal, 2-methylbutanal, 3-methylbutanal, 2,2-dimethylpropanal (none has CH₃CO–). Ketones: pentan-2-one ✔, 3-methylbutan-2-one ✔, pentan-3-one ✘. So 2.

pp.skill: Reactions of an aldehyde: HCN, reduction and tests
pp.stem: Butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, reacts in several ways.

parts.q: Butanal reacts with HCN in the presence of KCN. Describe the mechanism, including dipoles, lone pairs, curly arrows and the intermediate.
ms: C=O dipole (δ+ C); curly arrow from the lone pair on the C of CN⁻ to the δ+ C
curly arrow from the C=O π bond to O, giving the intermediate CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(O⁻)CN
curly arrow from O⁻ lone pair to H of HCN (H–CN bond breaks to CN⁻), giving CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CN

parts.q: The product of (a) is formed as a mixture of two optical isomers in equal amounts. Explain why.
ms: the C=O group (carbonyl carbon) is planar / trigonal
CN⁻ can attack from either side with equal probability, giving a racemic mixture

parts.q: Give the reagent and conditions to convert the product of (a) into a hydroxy carboxylic acid.
ms: heat under reflux with dilute HCl (or H₂SO₄)

parts.q: Write an equation for the reduction of butanal by NaBH₄, using [H], and name the product.
State what is seen when butanal is warmed with Tollens’ reagent, and explain why propanone gives no change.
ms: ketones have no H on the C=O carbon, so they cannot be oxidised (by mild oxidising agents)

pp.skill: Predicting test results for four C₄ compounds
pp.stem: Four compounds each contain four carbon atoms: W butanal, X butanone, Y butan-2-ol, Z 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

parts.q: Which two compounds turn warm acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ green?
Which two compounds give a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq)? State the formula of the precipitate.
Which two compounds give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH reagent?
Which two compounds fizz with sodium? Give the gas.
X reacts with HCN. Explain why the product has a chiral centre.
ms: the carbon bonded to OH and CN also carries CH₃ and C₂H₅: four different groups
